summary: A short correction to RFC 70: a statement in the FORTRAN program on page 7 should read N=1.

eli5.summary: A tiny fix to a note, like crossing out one wrong line in a recipe and writing the right one.

subtitle: A one-line correction to a FORTRAN program printed in RFC 70.

tldr.problem: A FORTRAN program printed on page 7 of RFC 70 contained a wrong statement.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC says that the second statement before statement 20 in that program should read N=1.
tldr.outcome: It is a correction note that updates RFC 70 and nothing else.

today: RFC 228 is a correction note to RFC 70. It is not obsoleted by any other RFC listed in the metadata.

sections.title: What This Note Corrects
sections.content:
RFC 228, titled Clarification, is a single-statement correction by Dave Walden of BBN, dated 22 September 1971. It updates RFC 70 and obsoletes nothing.

It concerns the FORTRAN program on page 7 of RFC 70.
sections.eli5: A short note saying that one line in an earlier note was wrong.

sections.title: The Corrected Statement
sections.content:
The RFC says that the second statement before statement 20 in the FORTRAN program on page 7 of RFC 70 should read N=1. That is the whole content of the document.

The note carries the categories B.2 and C.2 in its header. A closing note says it was put into machine readable form for the online RFC archives by BBN Corp. in December 1996.
sections.eli5: The wrong line should say N=1. That is all the note says.

sections.title: Why Such a Small RFC Exists
sections.content: Early RFCs were the working notes of the network community, and a correction was itself issued as an RFC with its own number. The text does not give any further background, so this RFC is best read together with the page it fixes in RFC 70.
sections.eli5: Even a tiny fix got its own numbered note so everyone could see it.
